sentences: Sorting waste, turning off the light when leaving a room, taking the bike instead of the car: we are often told that every little action counts for the planet.
But is that really true?
In the face of a problem as immense as climate change, are our individual efforts not insignificant?
The question is uncomfortable, and it deserves more than a simple answer.
Let's start with the objection, because it is serious.
If we add up all the emissions in the world, the portion that each individual can reduce through their daily actions is tiny.
While one person carefully saves water, a single factory, a single flight, or a single political decision can instantly negate the efforts of millions.
Worse still: by focusing on small actions, we risk forgetting what really matters.
Some large companies are actually quite happy to promote this idea, as it shifts the responsibility onto the consumer and leaves them off the hook.
Should we conclude that our actions are useless?
That would be jumping to conclusions, and it would be dangerous.
First, because these actions have a value that is not just mathematical.
Someone who changes their habits also changes their perspective: they become more attentive, more consistent, and harder to convince that 'nothing can be done.'
Next, because behaviors are contagious.
A habit, when it spreads, ends up changing the norms of an entire society, and then the decisions of those who govern us.
The real trap would be to choose between the two.

Pitting individual action against collective action is a false choice, and a choice that paralyzes: those who expect everything from governments do nothing themselves, and those who rely solely on small actions become discouraged when they discover their limits.
Yet the two feed off each other.
A citizen who acts in their life is also the one who votes, who talks to those around them, and who pushes companies and states to take action.
So, does one single action suffice?
No, obviously.
But framing the question this way is already a mistake.
The individual action was never meant to be enough; it is a starting point, not an end.
It matters not because it saves the planet on its own, but because it keeps us moving, and because nothing great, on a collective scale, has ever started without individuals deciding to act.

sentences: For the past two years, I've been buying almost everything second-hand: my clothes, my furniture, my books.
At first, it was to save money.
Now, it has become a pleasure.
It all started when I moved.
My apartment was empty and I only had four hundred euros to furnish it.
It was impossible to buy new.
So I looked on second-hand websites and at flea markets.
I found a table for thirty euros, four chairs for forty, and a sofa for eighty euros.
The sofa was a bit old, but very comfortable.
With new items, all of this would have cost me over a thousand euros.
I discovered two other advantages.
First, it's better for the environment.
When I buy an item that already exists, nothing new is made.
Then — and this is what I prefer — each item has a story.
My table comes from an old lady who was moving to the countryside.
She told me that her family had eaten around this table for thirty years.
Of course, you have to be patient.
You don't find exactly what you want right away.
You have to search, wait, and come back.
But when you find the right thing, it's a real victory.
Last month, I bought a bike for sixty euros.
It rides perfectly.
My friends often ask me: 'Where did you find that?'

The parents organized themselves quickly.
They created an association and collected four hundred fifty signatures in two weeks — almost the whole village.

sentences: I have lived in a big city for twelve years.
People often ask me if I like it, and I never manage to answer simply.
The truth is that the city gives a lot and takes a lot.
Let's start with what it gives.
Choice, first.
There are jobs, and not just a few: thousands, in very different fields.
When I wanted to change careers, I didn't need to move.
In my parents' village, it was impossible.
There is also culture.
A concert on a Tuesday night, an exhibition on a Sunday, a cinema showing films that no one knows.
I don't take advantage of it every week, far from it.
But knowing that it's possible changes something.
Finally, there's anonymity.
In a village, everyone knows what you are doing.
In the city, no one is watching you.
Depending on the person, it's either freedom or solitude.
Now, what it takes.
The noise, first, which never really stops.
The price, next: I pay for thirty-eight square meters what my brother pays for a house with a garden.
And fatigue, above all.
Crowded transport, queues, rushed people: everything requires a little effort, and these little efforts add up.
So, should we stay or leave?
I believe the question is poorly posed.
What matters is knowing what we came to find.
As for me, I came for work and for opportunities.
As long as I benefit from it, the city makes sense.
The day I pay this rent without getting anything in return, I will know it's time to leave.

sentences: We talk a lot about investment and quite a bit less about something more basic: precautionary savings, which means having a reserve of money available immediately in case of unexpected events.
The idea is nothing spectacular.
It's not about making your money grow, but about being able to absorb a shock: a broken car, a device to replace, a month with less income.
Its main interest is not financial, in fact.
It is strategic.
A person without a reserve suffers from unexpected events.
If their washing machine breaks down, they have to either go into debt at a high rate, accept the first available solution, or do without the machine.
None of these options is good, and all of them end up being expensive in the long run.
A person who has a reserve, even a modest one, can instead take the time to compare, wait for a cheaper repair, or refuse an unfavorable loan.
This is what specialists sometimes call 'the cost of poverty': being short on money forces you to make choices that, in fact, end up costing more.
How much should you set aside?
The advice varies, often between one and three months of regular expenses.
But this figure discourages a lot of people, who give up before they even start.
However, the essential point is elsewhere.
A reserve of five hundred euros already changes a lot of everyday situations.
The best advice I ever received was very simple: set aside a small amount automatically on payday, before spending anything.
What you don't see go by doesn't hurt.

sentences: According to estimates from the United Nations, nearly a third of the food produced in the world is never consumed.
This figure is hard to believe, yet it is well documented.
Waste does not occur in the same way depending on the countries.
In low-income countries, losses mainly happen before sale: poor storage conditions, slow transport, lack of a cold chain.
Food spoils before it arrives.
In wealthy countries, it's the opposite.
Most of the waste occurs at the end of the chain, in distribution and especially at home.
In France, it is estimated that each person throws away about thirty kilograms of food per year, including a portion that is still packaged.
The domestic causes are trivial: we buy too much, we forget what is at the back of the refrigerator, we cook portions that are too large, we confuse two date labels.
This confusion deserves to be clarified.
"To be consumed until" relates to safety: after this date, the product can be dangerous.
"To be consumed preferably before" relates to quality: the product remains consumable, it just loses some taste or texture.
Tons of rice, pasta, and perfectly good canned goods are thrown away because of this misunderstanding.
What works, in practice, comes down to a few things: planning meals for the week, making a list, putting older products in front, and considering leftovers as a planned meal rather than just scraps.
French law now prohibits large stores from throwing away consumable unsold goods; they must give them away.
This is a step forward.
But the main issue still lies in our kitchens.

sentences: In about ten years, cycling has significantly increased in most major French cities.
In some of them, the number of cyclists has more than doubled.
This change deserves to be analyzed, as it contradicts a widespread idea: that behaviors change mainly out of conviction.
What has driven change is not primarily awareness.
It's the infrastructure.
Studies on the subject are consistent.
The determining factor in the decision to cycle is neither ecology nor health: it's the feeling of safety.
As long as a journey involves riding among cars, the vast majority of people refuse — and this refusal is perfectly rational.
As soon as a protected and continuous bike lane exists, usage increases rapidly, including among people who did not consider themselves cyclists at all.
The important word is 'continuous'.
A bike lane that stops at a dangerous intersection is not a route: it's a section.
The cities that have been most successful have built coherent networks rather than isolated pieces.
The observed benefits exceed the avoided emissions.
Less noise, less air pollution, less congestion, and daily physical activity integrated effortlessly, which health authorities have been seeking for a long time.
There are also legitimate criticisms.
The developments sometimes come at the expense of pedestrians, or in already well-equipped neighborhoods, while peripheral areas remain dependent on cars.
The general lesson is clear, and it applies beyond cycling.
We change behaviors more effectively by making the right choice easy than by asking people to be better.

sentences: On most platforms, what we see is not what our neighbor sees.
An algorithm selects, for each person, the content deemed most likely to capture their attention.
The principle is not absurd: the amount of available content exceeds any human capacity to sort.
But the criterion used is problematic.
These systems do not optimize quality or truthfulness; they optimize engagement, meaning the time spent and reactions.
However, the content that generates the most reactions is not the most nuanced.
It is the most extreme, the most outrageous, the most emotional.
A balanced text, which acknowledges the complexity of a subject, struggles to circulate by its very nature.
We often talk about 'filter bubbles': each person would be trapped in a universe of opinions similar to their own.
Research suggests we should nuance this diagnosis.

sentences: Many people quietly admit that they find museums boring or tiring.
They feel a bit guilty, as if they lack culture.
The problem often comes more from the way of visiting than from the museum itself.
The most common mistake is wanting to see everything.
In front of a large museum displaying thousands of works, you move from room to room, look at each painting for a few seconds, and after two hours, you are exhausted without remembering anything.
Specialists sometimes call this 'museum fatigue,' and it is very real: attention collapses after a certain time.
The opposite approach works much better, and it is almost counterintuitive.
Choose a few, look for a long time.
Decide in advance to see five or ten works, not a hundred.
Sit in front of a painting for several minutes, let it affect you, notice the details, and come back.
You leave having seen fewer works, but with real memories.
Another key is the context.
A single work may seem silent; the same work, once you know its history or era, becomes expressive.
That’s why a guided tour, an audio guide, or simply some prior readings can radically change the experience.
Finally, it is not necessary to like it.
You can look carefully at a work, take an interest in it, and decide that it does not touch you.
This is a valid reaction, much more honest than polite and distracted admiration.
The museum is not an exam.
No one will check what you have remembered.
It is better to keep three vivid works than a hundred forgotten ones.

sentences: An urban planning idea has circulated a lot in recent years: the 'quarter-hour city.'
The principle is simple.
Everyone should be able to access the essentials of their daily needs — shops, school, doctor, work, leisure, green spaces — within fifteen minutes on foot or by bike.
It's not a completely new idea.
In reality, it's how most cities functioned before the automobile.
Neighborhoods mixed housing, shops, and workshops, and people lived close to everything.
The twentieth century separated these functions.
Residential areas were built on one side, commercial areas on the other, and office zones elsewhere, connected by cars.
This organization led to long daily commutes and total dependence on the automobile.
The quarter-hour city aims to mend this fabric: to bring functions closer together, promote walking and biking, and reduce forced travel.
The expected benefits are numerous: less pollution, more physical activity, revitalized local shops, and saved time.
But the concept is debated, and these criticisms deserve to be heard.
Some see it as an idea designed for wealthy city centers, difficult to apply in peripheral or rural areas where distances are large.
Others fear it will increase inequalities, with well-equipped neighborhoods becoming more desirable and more expensive.
There is also a common confusion to clear up: it's not about preventing people from leaving their neighborhood, but ensuring they aren't forced to for their daily needs.
The idea is therefore neither a utopia nor a threat.
It's a planning objective, easier to achieve in some cities than in others.
And a way to revisit an old question: how far do we live from our own lives?

sentences: In many families, grandparents play an essential role in taking care of children.
Picking them up from school, babysitting on Wednesdays, helping out when a child is sick: this largely invisible support represents a huge, unpaid contribution.
Without it, many parents simply couldn't work, as childcare options are either expensive or scarce.
This solidarity between generations benefits everyone.
For parents, it's material support and peace of mind: trusting someone with your child is priceless.
For children, it's an additional relationship, different from that of their parents, often more patient, filled with stories and family memories.
For the grandparents themselves, it's a role, a connection, a purpose — three things that protect against the isolation of old age.
But this help also experiences tensions, which are generally left unspoken.
Child-rearing methods have changed from one generation to the next: sugar, screens, rules, discipline.
Grandparents sometimes apply their own habits, parents get annoyed, and no one dares to speak frankly about it to avoid hurting feelings.
There is also the issue of boundaries.
Some grandparents feel obligated, to the point of sacrificing their own rest or plans.
The long-awaited retirement becomes filled with obligations.
Once again, the unspoken dominates.
Families that manage this arrangement well share one thing: they talk about it openly.
How many days, what rules, how to say no without guilt.
This help is not something owed.
It's a huge gift that deserves to be acknowledged as such — and discussed as such.

sentences: One can live for thirty years in a city without ever feeling that it belongs to us.
We work there, we sleep there, we move around there, but we pass through it more than we inhabit it.
This feeling, very common in contemporary large cities, raises a question that is far from obvious: what does it take to feel at home in a place, and not just to reside there?
The answer partly lies in public space.

A city is not just an addition of housing and offices; it is also made up of streets, squares, gardens, benches — all those places that do not belong to anyone in particular and thus, in a sense, belong to everyone.
This is where the feeling of belonging is played out.
Where public space is welcoming, we linger, we meet, we weave those tenuous connections that make a neighborhood feel like our own.
Where it shrinks, we just pass through.
However, this common space is today weakened.
It is shrinking under the pressure of cars, commerce, and sometimes fear.
We design places for consumption, not for staying without buying anything.
We multiply the measures that discourage sitting, lingering, or simply being there.
Little by little, the city stops offering places where one can exist for free, and with them disappears a part of what made it livable.
Feeling at home also implies having a say in one's living environment.
However, the decisions that shape a city — what is built there, what is demolished — often escape the residents.
They are rarely asked for their opinion, and when they are, it is sometimes just for show.
How can one appropriate a place that one has not helped to shape, and that can change overnight without our input?

The city will truly belong to us the day we stop being merely users and become residents again: people who have a place, a voice, and spaces to linger for no other reason than the pleasure of being there.
It is under this modest and demanding condition that a space becomes a home.

sentences: Many people experience this as they get older, without always daring to admit it: it becomes harder to make real friends.
Friendships from childhood and youth were formed almost effortlessly, supported by the daily proximity of school or studies.
In adulthood, this ease disappears, and one discovers that friendship, far from being automatic, now requires an attention that one never had to give it before.
The reasons for this are concrete.
Adult life scatters: we move, change jobs, start families, and free time becomes scarce.
The opportunities for regular meetings, which used to spark friendships without us thinking about it, become rare.
However, friendship needs time and repetition: you don't become close to someone you only see occasionally.
What used to be woven simply through the force of habit now requires intentional maintenance.
This evolution explains a discreet but widespread phenomenon: the slow disappearance of friendships that mattered.
Not due to quarrels or disagreements, but simply through neglect.
We don't argue; we gradually stop seeing each other.
Connections don't break suddenly; they unravel due to lack of maintenance, like a garden that one has stopped tending.
Recognizing this is not despairing; on the contrary, it's liberating.
For if adult friendship no longer arises on its own, it can still be built, provided one dedicates intention to it.
Proposing, following up, setting regular appointments, being the one to take the first step: these somewhat voluntary gestures are the price of friendship in adulthood.
They may seem artificial to those who long for the spontaneous bonds of the past, but they are, in reality, a form of loyalty.
One must also accept that not all friendships are meant to last, and that some fade naturally, without us having to feel guilty.
The important thing is not to hold on to everyone, but to nurture what truly matters.
Adult friendship may be less easy than that of youth, but it is no less precious — and the very fact that it requires effort gives it, in a sense, more value.
What we deliberately choose to cultivate is often worth more than what was simply given to us.

sentences: If someone breaks a leg, they consult without hesitation, receive treatment, and no one finds fault with that.

But if that same person suffers from anxiety, depression, or another mental disorder, everything becomes more complicated: shame gets involved, silence settles in, and seeking help, when it happens, often occurs late and reluctantly.
This difference in treatment between physical ailments and mental ones is one of the most persistent injustices in our relationship with health.
Where does this difference come from?
Partly from a long history of misunderstanding and prejudice.
For centuries, mental disorders have been misunderstood, surrounded by fear, associated with moral weakness, madness, and something shameful.
These representations, although declining, have not disappeared.

Many continue to believe, more or less consciously, that a mental disorder is a lack of willpower, that one just needs to 'pull themselves together' to feel better — as if one could cure depression solely through sheer willpower.
This belief is not only false but also dangerous.
Mental disorders are not weaknesses of character; they are real conditions that have their causes, mechanisms, and treatments, just like physical illnesses.
To impose a requirement of willpower is to add guilt to suffering and to divert those who suffer from the care that could help them.
Silence and shame literally kill by preventing people from asking for help.
It is therefore necessary to affirm an obvious truth that has been ignored for too long: mental health is a component of health, no more shameful and no less serious than physical health.
Suffering in your mind is no more dishonorable than suffering in your body, and seeking help is not an admission of weakness but an act of common sense and courage.
Consulting for a mental issue should be as natural as consulting for a physical issue.
Things are, fortunately, evolving.
People are talking more, understanding better, voices are gradually being freed, and public figures are daring to share their own struggles, helping to reduce shame.
This movement, still fragile, is heading in the right direction: it is slowly bringing the treatment of mental ailments closer to that of physical ailments.
Healing the mind like the body: this simple phrase summarizes the progress that still needs to be made.
As long as this is not an obvious truth for everyone, people will continue to suffer in silence, afraid to ask for help that would be readily given for any visible injury.

sentences: We almost always talk about aging in terms of loss: loss of vigor, health, beauty, and abilities.
This view is not false — aging does involve real losses that would be futile to deny.
But it is incomplete, as it overlooks what time can also bring.
Aging is not just about losing; it is also, sometimes, about gaining — understanding, finding peace, and shedding many illusions.
Recognizing this other side means rejecting a purely negative view of growing older.
The first gift of time is a certain wisdom — not automatic, but possible.
Having lived a long time, gone through trials, made mistakes and seen others make mistakes, all of this can teach what no book conveys: the knowledge of life, of others, and of oneself.
Those who have lived often know how to put into perspective what frightens the younger ones, distinguish the important from the secondary, and recognize that many dramas were not.
This practical wisdom, made of experience rather than knowledge, is one of the fruits that time can bear.
The second gift is a form of calm.
Youth is often troubled: by ambition, by the desire to prove oneself, by the worry of one's place, and by comparison to others.
With age, these troubles can calm down.
You have less to prove, less to conquer; you know your limits better and accept them; you compare yourself less, having learned the vanity of many pursuits.
This calm is not always present, but it is possible, and those who achieve it taste a serenity that troubled youth does not know.
Aging can mean shedding a weight.
The third gift, related to the previous ones, is a better perception of what matters.
Faced with the remaining time, which is shorter, we often stop wasting it on trivialities.

What seemed essential — success, recognition, accumulation — turns out to be secondary, while what we neglected — relationships, simple moments, the presence of loved ones — finally takes on its true value.
The passing time, by bringing us closer to the end, sometimes teaches us to live, by opening our eyes to what alone deserves our limited days.
It is not about idealizing old age or denying its sufferings.
Aging also brings challenges, and wisdom, calm, and clarity are not guaranteed: one can age bitter, fearful, without having learned anything.
These gifts of time are not automatic; they require that we consent to them, that we accept aging rather than refuse it.
But they are possible, and those who receive them testify that there is, in growing older, something other than decline.
What time teaches us is perhaps, at its core, how to live — sometimes too late, but not always.
And this lesson, elders could pass on to the younger ones, if we knew how to listen to them.

For in a society obsessed with youth and hurried to live, the voice of those who have traversed time has something irreplaceable to say: that life is brief, that it is precious, and that it is better to understand this sooner rather than later.

sentences: A strange paradox characterizes our time: we have never been so connected, and yet, loneliness has never seemed so widespread.
We can reach anyone at any moment, we have hundreds of 'contacts', and we are constantly connected to a vast network of other people.
And yet, the feeling of loneliness, real isolation, is gaining ground, to the point that some speak of a true epidemic.
How can we explain that so many connections are accompanied by so much loneliness?
The answer likely lies in a confusion between two very different things: being in contact and being connected.
Our technologies multiply contacts — messages, reactions, brief exchanges — but these contacts do not necessarily create true connections.
One can exchange a hundred messages a day without having a deep relationship with anyone; one can have thousands of 'friends' online and have no one to confide in about what really matters.
The quantity of contacts has exploded; the quality of connections, however, does not keep pace, and sometimes even declines.
There is more.
These constant contacts can feed loneliness instead of fulfilling it.
By giving the illusion of relationship, they relieve us of the need to seek real ones; by occupying time and attention, they leave less room for real, more demanding encounters.
One can spend evenings scrolling through the lives of others on a screen, ultimately feeling an even greater emptiness.
Easy contact then becomes a depleting substitute for difficult connection, a way of being with others without truly being with them.
To this is added a more subtle effect.
By constantly seeing, on screens, the apparently fulfilled lives of others — their parties, their successes, their staged happiness — we feel, by contrast, more alone and more inadequate.
The constant comparison with idealized existences deepens the feeling of being, oneself, on the sidelines, excluded from a conviviality that others seem to enjoy.
Permanent connection does not show us the loneliness of others, as real as our own; it shows us their chosen moments, and leaves us alone with our ordinary lives.
Should we conclude that these technologies are the cause of our loneliness, and that we should turn away from them?
That would be too simple.
They can also truly connect, maintain valuable links despite distance, and break the isolation of some.
The problem is not the tool, but the use that substitutes contact for connection, and connection for presence.

What we lack is not means of communication, which we have in abundance; it is deep relationships, which require time, presence, and an attention that constant contact tends, on the contrary, to scatter.
Thus, escaping this loneliness in the midst of the crowd does not mean cutting ourselves off from others, but distinguishing contact from connection, and cultivating the latter.

This means prioritizing a few deep relationships over a multitude of superficial contacts; offering real presence rather than constant and distracted availability; accepting the demands of true connection, which cannot be established with a click.
Being truly with someone, in a world of endless contacts, has become both rarer and more precious.

sentences: There is a boundary that rigorous thinking must constantly remind us of, as it is frequently crossed: the one that separates what is from what ought to be, facts from values, science from morality.
Science, powerful as it may be, establishes what is the case; it is inherently incapable of saying, on its own, what ought to be done.
From the observation that something is, one can never deduce, through logic alone, that it ought or ought not to be.
This boundary, often overlooked, is nonetheless crucial, and its confusion is the source of serious misguidance.
Let us clearly understand what this limit means.
Science can tell us what the effects of an action are, what means allow us to achieve an end, what will happen if we do this or that.
But it cannot tell us what end we should pursue, what is worth seeking, what is right or good.
It can establish that a policy will have a certain result; it cannot establish that this result is desirable.
It can describe what human nature is; it cannot deduce how we should live from that.
Between the observation of what is and the judgment of what ought to be, there is a leap that no observation, no measurement, can bridge.
This limit is not a weakness of science, but a characteristic of the nature of questions.
Value questions are not poorly resolved factual questions that an increase in science would eventually settle; they belong to a different order.
No experiment will tell us whether freedom is better than security, whether equality should take precedence over merit, or whether a human life has infinite value.
These questions engage what we hold to be important, what we choose to value, and pertain to moral and political deliberation, not to scientific demonstration.
Science informs these choices; it does not replace them.
Overlooking this boundary leads to two symmetrical and equally dangerous errors.
The first consists of making science say what it cannot say, asking it to resolve value questions, and presenting political or moral choices as scientific conclusions.
"Science shows that we must do this": this very common phrase almost always masks a leap from fact to value, presenting a subjective choice as an objective necessity.
This confusion is all the more insidious as it dresses preferences as truths and removes from debate, under the guise of science, what should be discussed.
The second, inverse error consists of disqualifying science on the grounds that it does not say everything, rejecting what it establishes because it does not resolve value questions.

"Science cannot tell us how to live, so its authority is not superior": this reasoning confuses the two levels in the opposite direction and is often used to dismiss inconvenient facts in the name of what science does not claim to do.
That science does not say what ought to be does not weaken what it establishes about what is; it is even by respecting its limit that we best recognize its authority in its own domain.
Firmly maintaining the boundary between fact and value is therefore to do justice to both science and morality, assigning each its domain.
To science, the rigorous establishment of what is, with the authority that comes with it; to human deliberation, the judgment on what ought to be, which no knowledge can exempt us from assuming.

This distribution does not diminish science; it preserves it from uses that would distort it and protects human freedom from the temptation to offload its choices onto a supposed scientific necessity.
For deciding what we ought to do, what we want to strive for, will always remain our task and our responsibility — a task that science can illuminate, but will never take away from us.

sentences: Inequality is at the heart of our political debates, yet we often confuse two questions that need to be distinguished: whether inequalities exist and whether they are just.
For not all inequality is necessarily an injustice, and not every reduction of inequalities is necessarily a step towards justice.

Untangling these questions is essential for thinking clearly about a topic that political passion tends to muddle, where everyone sees their own position as obvious and that of the opponent as outrageous.
Let’s start by acknowledging that there are inequalities that hardly shock our sense of justice.

The idea that someone who works harder, takes more risks, and contributes more should receive more does not seem unjust in itself; many see it as a requirement of justice, one that rewards effort and merit.
A strict equality that would treat equally someone who dedicates themselves and someone who does nothing would indeed clash with our sense of fairness.
Thus, there are inequalities that seem just, or at least acceptable, because they reflect differences we deem relevant.
However, this justification has limits that examination quickly reveals.
Real inequalities reflect only very partially merit or effort.
A large part of inequalities stems from factors for which no one is responsible: birth, environment, inheritance, innate talents, luck.
Someone born into a privileged environment benefits from advantages they did not earn; someone born into poverty suffers disadvantages for which they are not to blame.
Inequalities that result not from individuals' choices but from the lottery of birth are much harder to justify: how can it be fair that the randomness of birth determines the fate of an entire life?
Thus, a first criterion emerges to distinguish just inequalities from unjust ones: that of responsibility.

An inequality that results from individuals' free choices, their efforts, and what they are responsible for can be considered just, or at least legitimate; an inequality that arises from circumstances for which they are not responsible — birth, luck — calls for more correction.

This appealing criterion, however, does not resolve everything, as it is terribly difficult to untangle, in a trajectory, the part of choices from that of circumstances: does not someone who has 'made efforts' owe it, in part, to an education that instilled in them a taste for effort?
The boundary between what one is responsible for and what one has received is blurred, and merit, upon examination, partly dissolves into circumstances.
A second criterion concerns the effects of inequality on the most disadvantaged.

One can argue that an inequality is acceptable if it ultimately benefits everyone, including the most deprived — for example, if by rewarding the most productive, it stimulates an activity from which the poorest also benefit.
But if an inequality worsens the plight of the most disadvantaged, trapping some in misery to allow others to thrive, it becomes difficult to justify.
According to this criterion, inequality is acceptable only insofar as it serves the interest of all, not just that of the privileged at the expense of others.
These criteria do not provide a simple answer, and the debate on the justice of inequalities remains open, as it involves values that are prioritized differently according to beliefs.

But they allow us to move beyond two equally simplistic positions: one that considers all inequality just, on the grounds that it reflects merit, while it largely stems from unearned circumstances; and one that deems all inequality unjust, in the name of an egalitarianism that ignores legitimate differences.
The truth is more nuanced: some inequalities are just, others are not, and the challenge is to distinguish between them.
Refusing this distinction, in either direction, is to avoid thinking about justice in favor of a slogan.

sentences: We do not build ourselves alone.

The idea that we would be an autonomous 'self', forming independently of others, is an illusion: from childhood and throughout life, we construct ourselves under the gaze of others, through the way others see us, judge us, and recognize us.
This gaze of others is constitutive of who we are, and this dependence is ambivalent: it can be a blessing, a source of recognition and existence, or an alienation, a prison in which one gets lost.
Understanding this relationship is essential for thinking about identity.
Let’s first consider what the gaze of others has that is constitutive.
We become aware of ourselves largely through others: it is by being seen, named, and judged that we form an image of ourselves.
A child is shaped by the gaze of their parents; an adult is partly defined by how their surroundings perceive them.
We need to be recognized, seen, and confirmed in our existence by the gaze of others; without this recognition, our very identity wavers.
The gaze of others is therefore not a mere external addition; it contributes to making us who we are.
This dependence can be a blessing.
Being recognized, loved, and appreciated by others confirms our worth, gives us a place, and nourishes our self-esteem.
The benevolent gaze of others makes us exist, supports us, and allows us to unfold.
We need to be seen to feel real, recognized to feel worthy.

In this sense, the gaze of others is not a constraint, but a source: we build ourselves in and through mutual recognition, and this interdependence is the very fabric of our social existence and identity.
But this same gaze can become an alienation.
For by depending too much on the gaze of others, one risks losing oneself in it, existing only through it, and conforming one's being to what others expect or approve.

Those who excessively care about the image they project, who adjust their behavior based on the judgment of others, who exist only in approval, are prisoners of the gaze of others, alienated to an image that is no longer their own.
The gaze that could confirm then becomes a prison, where one disguises oneself to please, where one forgets oneself to meet expectations.
The recognition sought at all costs turns into servitude.
This alienation is exacerbated by our time, which has made self-exposure a permanent practice.

In a world where everyone constantly puts themselves on display, where one seeks approval through carefully staged images of oneself, dependence on the gaze of others reaches an unprecedented intensity.
We live under the supposed gaze of others, we adjust our existence based on the image we project, we measure our worth by the approval received.
This constant exposure, far from liberating, can trap us in an anxious quest for recognition, where we lose ourselves in the desire to be seen.
The issue is therefore not to free ourselves from the gaze of others — which is impossible and would not be desirable, as we need recognition — but to find a proper relationship to it.

This requires welcoming the recognition of others without becoming enslaved to it, taking into account the gaze of others without surrendering one's being to it, and maintaining, under the gaze, a relationship to oneself that does not depend entirely on it.
It is about existing through others without losing oneself in them, being recognized without renouncing oneself.
This difficult balance — welcoming the gaze without becoming alienated by it — is one of the conditions for an identity that is both connected to others and true to itself.
For we construct ourselves in the gaze of others, but we must not dissolve into it.

sentences: Few concepts are as frequently invoked and as poorly understood as secularism.

People claim it in contradictory ways: some see it as the neutrality of the state towards all beliefs, others as a means to push religion out of the public space, and still others as a kind of identity to defend against certain beliefs.
These divergent, often controversial uses obscure an idea that deserves clarification, as it relates to how a society allows different beliefs to coexist.
What does secularism really mean, and what does it require?
At its core, secularism refers to a certain organization of the relationship between the state and religious or philosophical beliefs.
It is based on two interconnected ideas: the separation of the state and religions, and the neutrality of the state towards them.
The secular state does not claim any religion, does not favor or persecute any, and guarantees everyone the freedom to believe or not believe.
This neutrality of the state is the condition for equal freedom for all: because the state does not take sides, everyone can live their beliefs without being favored or oppressed.
Secularism, in this primary sense, is a principle of freedom and equality, not of restriction.
This clarification helps to correct a common misunderstanding.
Secularism is not hostility towards religion, nor its exclusion from the public space.
It does not require religious beliefs to be hidden, nor that the public space be emptied of any expression of belief; it requires that the state be neutral, not that citizens must be.
Neutrality applies to public authority and those who embody it, not to individuals, who remain free to express their beliefs.

Confusing the neutrality of the state with an obligation of neutrality imposed on citizens distorts secularism, turning it into an instrument of restriction of the freedom it is supposed to guarantee.
A second misunderstanding treats secularism as a kind of belief among others, or even as an identity to defend against certain beliefs.
But secularism is not a belief that opposes religions; it is the framework that allows all beliefs to coexist.
It is not part of the debate of beliefs, but above it, like the referee who guarantees each its place without adopting any.

Turning it into an identity opposed to certain beliefs, a weapon against this or that religion, is to turn it against itself: from a principle of neutrality and coexistence, it becomes an instrument of division and exclusion.
Secularism distorted into a militant identity ceases to be secularism.
These misunderstandings are not innocent; they often serve controversial intentions.
Invoking secularism to restrict religious freedom, to target a certain belief, to impose a form of conformity, is to instrumentalize a principle of freedom for the sake of exclusion.
True secularism is demanding precisely because it also protects beliefs that are unpopular, guaranteeing the freedom of those whose expression one would want to restrict.
It is not in the service of one camp, but of the coexistence of all; distorting it into a weapon against some is to betray what makes it valuable.

Understanding secularism means restoring it to its principle: not hostility towards religion, not a militant identity, but the neutrality of the state that guarantees everyone equal freedom to believe or not.
Understood this way, it is one of the most beautiful inventions for peacefully coexisting incompatible beliefs, by removing the state from their quarrel.
Its difficulty, and its greatness, lies in protecting the freedom of all, including those whose beliefs we do not share.

To truly defend it is to reject the uses that distort it, and to remember that it is a principle of freedom before being anything else — especially not a weapon against the freedom it is meant to guarantee.

sentences: Instant access to a vast amount of human knowledge has transformed our relationship with knowledge and presents an unprecedented challenge to education.
Since all information is now available in an instant, what is the point of learning, memorizing, and accumulating knowledge?
Wouldn't it be enough to know how to search for information and find it when we need it, rather than to carry it within ourselves?
This question, made urgent by the ease of access, forces us to rethink what learning means in the information age and why it remains necessary.
The argument for reducing the burden of learning has its apparent strength.
Why overload memory with knowledge that is available with a click?
Isn't it better to free the mind from this burden, teaching it to find information rather than to retain it, to navigate knowledge rather than to possess it?

This appealing notion suggests that in the information age, the focus should no longer be on learning content, which is destined to be available, but on skills: knowing how to search, sort, and use information.
Knowledge would be found outside, in machines; it would just require knowing how to access it.
However, this idea encounters a decisive objection that we have already faced: we do not think with available information, but with what we know.

To understand information, to judge it, to integrate it, one must have prior knowledge that allows it to make sense; information is only interpreted against the backdrop of already acquired knowledge.
A mind empty of knowledge would not know what to do with available information; it could neither understand it, nor sort it, nor critique it, lacking the knowledge necessary to evaluate it.
Far from making learning superfluous, the abundance of information makes it more necessary: because to navigate this mass, one needs solid knowledge to serve as a compass.
There is more.
The much-praised skill of 'knowing how to search and sort information' is not a formal skill, independent of content; it precisely requires knowledge.

To judge the reliability of information, one must know the field; to distinguish the true from the false, one needs reference points; to sort the relevant from the trivial, one must understand what is at stake.

Claiming to train minds capable of sorting information without imparting knowledge is like trying to build without foundations: sorting information is only possible for those who already know, and the ignorant, overwhelmed by the mass, cannot find their way.
Access to information does not replace knowledge; it requires it.
This does not mean that the information age changes nothing about what needs to be learned.
Some knowledge, once essential, may be less necessary when it is easily available; the emphasis may shift from memorizing details to understanding principles, structures, and methods.
But this shift does not exempt one from learning; it alters what we learn and how, without eliminating the need for internalized knowledge.

The information age does not render learning obsolete; it redefines its object, perhaps refocusing it on the essentials: fundamental knowledge, frameworks that enable understanding, and methods that allow for judgment.
Learning in the information age remains necessary, perhaps more than ever.

For in a world saturated with information of all quality, where the true coexists with the false, and where the mass overwhelms any processing capacity, what distinguishes the educated mind from the unprepared mind is precisely the internalized knowledge that allows one to navigate, judge, and understand.
Universal access to information does not equalize minds; it widens the gap between those who know and can benefit from it, and those who, lacking knowledge, drown in it.
True freedom in the information age does not belong to those who can find everything, but to those who know enough to understand what they find.
That is why learning, far from being rendered superfluous, remains the condition for autonomy in a world of endless information.

sentences: At the end of this meditation on solitude, the knowledge of others, love, and desire, one image can bring together what we have glimpsed: that of love as the meeting of two solitudes that recognize and protect each other.
A poet wrote that love consists in this: that two solitudes protect, limit, and greet each other.

This formula, of striking depth, expresses what the highest love can be: not the abolition of each person's solitude in a fusion, but the respectful meeting of two beings who remain, at their core, distinct and alone, and who love each other precisely in this mutual recognition of their solitude.
This conception opposes a widespread image of love: that of fusion, of union which would abolish distance, make two beings one, and dissolve each person's solitude in total communion.
This image of love-fusion has its allure; it expresses the desire to escape one's solitude, to merge with the other, to no longer be two.
But it may be a delusion, and even a danger.
For fusion, if it were possible, would abolish what gives each person their value: their uniqueness, their individuality, their own being.

To want to completely merge with the other, or to absorb them into oneself, is in a sense to wish for their disappearance as a distinct being; love-fusion, taken to its extreme, is possessive, devouring, and denies the otherness of the beloved instead of respecting it.
Love as the meeting of two solitudes is something entirely different.
It does not seek to abolish distance, to merge beings, or to deny their essential solitude; it recognizes, respects, and protects it.

To love in this way is not to want to possess the other, to absorb them, to make them one's own; it is to recognize their otherness, their freedom, their solitude, and to love them in that very distance that makes them different.
Two solitudes that greet each other: each remains itself, distinct, with its mystery and freedom, and it is across this respected distance that they meet, recognize, and love each other.

This love does not fill the essential solitude — we have seen that nothing can — but it transforms it: from a solitude endured, it becomes a solitude inhabited by the presence of the other, recognized and shared.
This conception of love has profound implications for the way we love.
It invites us to respect the freedom of the beloved, not to want to possess, control, or confine them to our own idea of them; to allow them their mystery, their uniqueness, their own space.
It invites us to love the other as other, not as an extension of ourselves, a mirror, or an object to possess; to rejoice in their otherness rather than wanting to diminish it.
It invites us to that ultimate delicacy which consists of protecting the solitude of the beloved as much as our own, not to invade, to maintain the distance that allows each to remain themselves.
The greatest respect in love is perhaps that which recognizes in the beloved a being who does not belong to us, a freedom that we do not possess, a solitude that we cannot and must not abolish.
This way of loving is more demanding than the ideal of fusion, and undoubtedly rarer.
For it is easier to want to possess, absorb, and merge than to respect the otherness, to protect the distance, and to love the other in their freedom.

Fusion flatters the desire to escape oneself, to abolish one's solitude; the respect for two solitudes requires maturity, generosity, and a renunciation of possession, which are the fulfillment of love rather than its starting point.

But it is in this demand that the greatness of true love resides: not in the impossible abolition of solitude, but in its recognition and respect; not in the fusion that denies the other, but in the encounter that honors them.

Thus, the highest love is not the one that claims to abolish essential solitude, which is impossible and would deny each person's uniqueness; it is the one that, by recognizing it, transforms it into a solitude inhabited by the presence of the other, in an encounter where two distinct beings greet and protect each other across the distance that makes them different.

This conception reconciles what we have glimpsed: the essential solitude that cannot be abolished, the knowledge of others that respects their mystery, the love that sees and brings forth, the desire that gives rather than takes.

It states that the highest relationship between beings is not the fusion that denies their solitude, but the love that recognizes and honors it — two solitudes that, knowing themselves to be irreducible, nonetheless choose to meet, to protect each other, to greet each other, and find in this respectful encounter, more than in any fusion, the truth and beauty of love.

sentences: Every spring, many museums across the country open their doors for free for an entire night as part of a very popular cultural event called the Night of Museums.
This event has been happening for several years and attracts, with each edition, an increasingly large and diverse audience.
The idea behind this event is simple: to allow everyone, regardless of their budget, to discover the museum collections in a different atmosphere from that of the daytime.
At night, the exhibition halls take on a special, almost mysterious atmosphere that completely changes how visitors perceive the works of art.
In large cities, some museums offer special guided tours led by passionate curators who share surprising anecdotes about the paintings and sculptures on display.
Other museums organize concerts of classical or contemporary music directly in the halls, creating an original dialogue between the artworks and the music played live.
Children are not forgotten during this exceptional evening.
Several museums set up creative workshops where younger children can draw, paint, or even try sculpture with the help of professional artists.
These activities help spark artistic curiosity from a young age, in a fun and pressure-free environment.
A regular visitor of the event shares that he looks forward to this evening eagerly every year.
He explains that the crowd, the music, and the special lights completely transform his relationship with art.
According to him, he often discovers works that he had seen before from a completely new perspective.
Natural history museums also participate in the event, with activities related to astronomy or biology.
Some even organize stargazing on their rooftop terrace, weather permitting, in collaboration with local amateur astronomer associations.
This cultural event sees growing success each year.
According to the organizers, several million visitors take part in this special night across Europe, making it one of the most attended cultural events on the continent.
This success shows that culture, when made accessible and free, continues to attract a very large and diverse audience.
For the museums themselves, this evening also represents a unique opportunity to reach an audience that might never visit their collections under normal circumstances.
Many visitors thus discover cultural places in their own city that they did not know about before, and then return to visit them during the year, outside of this exceptional event.

sentences: A question I often ask myself is: do I dress for myself, or for the gaze of others?
In the morning, before an important meeting, I choose my clothes carefully.
I wonder what the person across from me will think of me.
It's not just a matter of comfort.
Some days, on the contrary, at home, alone, I dress without thinking.
An old sweater, comfortable pants.
No one is watching me, so why pay attention?
This difference made me realize that dressing is never completely neutral.
Even when we think we dress 'for ourselves', we actually carry the gaze of others within us, like an internalized habit.
My sister, on the other hand, claims to dress solely for her own pleasure, without caring about others.
I believe her to some extent.
But I also think that none of us completely escapes this external gaze, even if it's imaginary.
This pressure actually varies depending on the groups: a family dinner and a night out with friends call for different outfits, although I can't always say why.
Each circle seems to carry slightly different expectations for me, almost instinctively fulfilled, without me really thinking about it.
Maybe true freedom isn't about completely ignoring this gaze, which seems almost impossible, but about consciously choosing how much we let it influence our choices.
As for me, I continue to dress differently depending on the situation.
And I'm no longer sure that it's a problem.

sentences: Before choosing a film, I always used to check professional reviews published in newspapers or specialized magazines.
Today, this habit has almost disappeared for me, replaced by ratings given by other viewers on websites, or simply by recommendations from an algorithm.
This change raises an interesting question: do professional critics still have a role in how we choose a film?
Some arguments support their case.
An experienced critic has an in-depth knowledge of cinema, an analytical ability that the average viewer may not necessarily have.
But other arguments work against them.
Public ratings, although less expert individually, represent the average of thousands of opinions, which can provide a more accurate picture of a film's actual reception.

Moreover, some professional critics sometimes have tastes that are very different from the general public, making their opinions less useful for someone simply looking for a good moment of relaxation.
Before spending money on a ticket, I now check both sources: the opinion of a recognized critic and the average public ratings.
This double-checking, which takes a bit longer than an impulsive decision, at least saves me from the most predictable disappointments, without taking away the pleasure of a personal discovery.
I believe, for my part, that both approaches have their usefulness, depending on what you're looking for.
For a demanding art film, the opinion of a critic remains valuable.

sentences: The demand for performance, long associated with high-level sports, has gradually expanded to much broader areas of our lives.

Schools now evaluate their students based on increasingly precise numerical indicators; companies measure their employees' productivity with tools worthy of tracking a professional athlete; even our leisure activities are sometimes transformed into challenges to optimize, tracked by an app on our phones.
This spread of sports vocabulary and methods into everyday life deserves our attention.
Where does this collective fascination for the constant measurement of our performances come from, even in areas that historically have never been thought of in this competitive logic?
One possible explanation lies in the reassuring appeal of measurement itself: a number seems objective, indisputable, and easier to communicate than a nuanced and complex assessment.
It's simpler to announce that a student scores fifteen out of twenty than to explain in detail their actual progress, specific difficulties, and less measurable qualities.
However, this widespread quantification is not without consequences.

Researchers in work and educational psychology observe a significant increase in performance-related anxiety among younger generations, who are faced from childhood with a constant evaluation of their results, continually compared to those of others.
Should we then completely reject this culture of performance, partly inherited from the sports world?
That would likely be excessive: measurement also allows for objective progress and helps identify real weaknesses to correct.

But perhaps it would be wise to also find a more important place in sports for what escapes numerical measurement: the simple pleasure of effort, patient learning, and perseverance that does not immediately translate into a measurable result.
Without this balance, performance risks becoming, in schools and elsewhere, a source of exhaustion rather than a true driver of progress.

sentences: Before the widespread use of artificial lighting, night represented, for most of humanity, a period of rest largely imposed by the darkness itself, which naturally limited the activities possible once the sun had set.
The gradual arrival of electric lighting, starting from the end of the nineteenth century, disrupted this millennia-old organization of human time.
For the first time in history, it became possible to indefinitely extend daytime activities well after nightfall, without relying on costly and limited sources of light like candles or oil lamps.
This transformation, often celebrated as an undeniable progress, had less visible consequences on our physiology.
The human body, shaped by millennia of evolution in sync with the natural cycle of day and night, did not adapt as quickly as our technological environment.

Researchers in chronobiology have notably shown that exposure to artificial light in the evening, particularly that emitted by modern screens, disrupts the natural secretion of melatonin, the hormone that signals to our body that it is time to prepare for sleep.
This disruption would thus delay, for many people, the natural onset of sleep by several tens of minutes, or even more.

This situation illustrates a broader gap between our biology, which remains fundamentally ancient, and a technological environment in constant evolution, capable of profoundly altering rhythms that humanity had nonetheless respected, often without even thinking about it consciously, for most of its history.

sentences: Democratic deliberation, as conceived by political philosophers from the Enlightenment to contemporary theorists of deliberative democracy, requires a specific set of conditions that the current digital space seems to systematically undermine in many ways, without it being certain that a reconstruction of these conditions is still possible within the current technological framework.
The first of these conditions, as we have seen, is the existence of a common space where citizens, exposed to the same information, can confront their differing interpretations of a shared reality.

The algorithmic fragmentation of our informational environments has significantly weakened this condition by replacing the relative unity of the past with an increasing plurality of increasingly isolated informational worlds, where disagreement no longer only concerns the interpretation of facts, but the facts themselves.

The second condition relates to the recognition of equal legitimacy among interlocutors, a condition that is all the more fragile given that the relative anonymity offered by many platforms, combined with the absence of immediate social consequences for incivility, fosters a rhetorical brutality rarely tolerated in face-to-face conversation.
This erosion of civility, far from being anecdotal, directly undermines the presumption of good faith without which no authentic deliberation can truly take place.

The third condition, more subtle, concerns the time necessary for any serious reflection: deliberating requires the ability to suspend judgment, examine contradictory arguments, and sometimes change one's mind after careful consideration.

The very architecture of social networks, organized around the immediacy of reaction and the brevity of format, seems structurally inhospitable to this long time of deliberation, favoring instead the rapid expression of an already formed opinion rather than its patient reconsideration.
Should we conclude from this accumulated observation that authentic democratic deliberation has become outright impossible in the digital age?
Such a conclusion, as tempting as it may be in its radicality, deserves to be nuanced by at least two considerations.

First, the same tools that fragment and polarize have also allowed, in certain well-documented contexts, the emergence of informed citizen mobilizations and public debates of an unprecedented scale and diversity of participants, suggesting that the problem lies less in the technology itself than in the design choices that currently shape it.

Finally, none of the defeated conditions is irretrievably lost: they could, in principle, be restored through different technical, regulatory, and cultural choices, if the collective will to restore them were to form widely enough.

This reformulation also invites us to reconsider the role of the ordinary citizen, too often reduced, in this debate, to the position of a passive user subjected to architectures that they did not design.

In principle, nothing prevents the emergence of a collective citizen demand, driven by a sufficient mass of users, calling for different platforms, differently oriented algorithms, and regulation that meets the real democratic stakes — provided that this demand itself manages to carve out a path in a digital space that we have seen structurally favors immediacy over long-term reflection.

The question posed by this title therefore calls for less a definitive answer than a reformulation: not 'can we still deliberate,' as if the answer depended on a technological fate already sealed, but 'do we still want, collectively, to create the conditions for authentic deliberation,' which shifts the question from the realm of technology to the more uncomfortable but also more fruitful territory of political and cultural will.

For current platforms are not laws of nature, but constructed artifacts, shaped by choices that could, in principle, be undone or redone differently — provided that enough citizens come to demand, for the digital public space, the same standards of deliberative quality that they also demand for their oldest political institutions.

sentences: We spontaneously consider forgetting to be the enemy of memory, its defeat, the failure of a faculty that, when well exercised, should retain everything.

This conception, deeply rooted in common sense, even permeates our vocabulary: we talk about "losing" a memory, about "failing" memory, as if forgetting were merely a regrettable subtraction from a reservoir that, by default, should remain complete.
However, contemporary neuroscience invites us to almost entirely overturn this intuition.

Far from being a mere accident, an involuntary leak of information that a better-designed mechanism should have prevented, forgetting is an active, regulated process with multiple functions that are largely beneficial for the organism that exercises it.

The brain does not simply passively let go of what it cannot retain; it actively selects, at every moment, deliberately erasing a considerable amount of information to preserve the ability to effectively process what remains.

This selective function of forgetting responds to a basic computational necessity: a system that retained everything, without discrimination, without ever erasing anything, would quickly be overwhelmed by a deluge of details without hierarchy, unable to distinguish the essential from the trivial, the relevant information from the accumulated noise.

It has been observed in very rare individuals with a so-called hypermnesic memory, who can remember with extraordinary precision almost every day lived, that this is not an enviable gift, but often a burden: the inability to distinguish, in this unbroken flow of equally vivid memories, what truly deserves attention from what is merely an insignificant anecdote, paradoxically producing less fluid thinking, less capable of generalizing, abstracting, and drawing synthetic lessons from accumulated experience.

Forgetting also fulfills a less often recognized but equally essential function: that of allowing forgiveness, reconciliation, and even the possibility of continuing to live alongside those who have hurt us, or of ourselves as we were in moments we are no longer proud of.

An absolute memory, which would retain with equal intensity every offense, every humiliation, every failure, would undoubtedly make social life, and inner life itself, considerably more difficult to bear.

The gradual fading of the emotional burden attached to a painful memory, a phenomenon that psychology sometimes refers to as therapeutic forgetting, does not constitute a denial of what was experienced, but a necessary condition for life to continue without being crushed by the cumulative weight of all that it has entailed that is painful.

This individual dynamic resonates strikingly on a collective scale: societies themselves practice a selective forgetting of their own history, highlighting certain episodes while allowing others to fade, in a process that is reminiscent, on a different scale, of the mechanisms of individual memory.

Some historians see it as a necessity comparable to that which operates in individuals: a nation that would retain with equal intensity every conflict, every division, every wound of its past could hardly project itself collectively into the future.

Others, on the contrary, denounce this selective collective forgetting as a real danger, the risk of repeating mistakes precisely because we have ceased to remember them vividly enough to draw a lasting lesson.
Should we then completely abandon the ancient ideal of a faithful memory, cultivated and maintained against the natural erosion of time?

Certainly not: there is a fundamental difference between the selective and welcome forgetting of what does not need to be retained, and the regrettable loss of what, on the contrary, deserves to be preserved — a precious memory, hard-earned knowledge, a lesson whose forgetting would expose us to repeating the same mistakes.

Wisdom, in matters of memory, probably does not consist in fighting forgetting in general, which would be both vain and counterproductive, but in learning to distinguish what deserves to be actively cultivated from what forgetting, left to its natural course, fortunately takes care of erasing for us, thus freeing us from a burden that no human memory could indefinitely bear without being crushed.

sentences: A group of about fifteen men, aged between twenty-five and forty, scattered among the dancers or chatting at the entrance, stood out from the crowd by a familial air, regardless of their differences in age, attire, or appearance.
Their clothes, better tailored, seemed to be made of a softer fabric, and their hair, styled in curls towards the temples, was polished with finer pomades.

They had the complexion of wealth, that white complexion enhanced by the pallor of porcelain, the sheen of satin, the varnish of fine furniture, and maintained in good health by a discreet diet of exquisite foods.

Their necks turned comfortably in low cravats; their long sideburns fell over turned-down collars; they wiped their lips with handkerchiefs embroidered with a large monogram, from which a sweet fragrance emanated.
Those who were starting to age looked young, while something mature spread across the faces of the young.

In their indifferent gazes floated the tranquility of passions satisfied daily; and, beneath their gentle manners, pierced that particular brutality communicated by the dominance of somewhat easy things, where strength is exerted and vanity is amused, such as handling thoroughbred horses and associating with fallen women.
Three steps away from Emma, a rider in a blue coat was discussing Italy with a pale young woman wearing a pearl necklace.
They praised the size of the pillars of Saint Peter's, Tivoli, Vesuvius, Castellamare and the Cassines, the roses of Genoa, and the Colosseum by moonlight.
Emma listened with one ear to a conversation full of words she did not understand.
They surrounded a very young man who had beaten Miss Arabelle and Romulus the week before, winning two thousand louis for jumping a ditch in England.
One complained about his runners getting fat; another about printing errors that had distorted the name of his horse.
The atmosphere of the ball was heavy; the lamps were dimming.
People were flowing back into the billiard room.
A servant climbed onto a chair and broke two windows; at the sound of the shattering glass, Madame Bovary turned her head and saw, against the panes, the faces of peasants watching.
Then the memory of the Bertaux came to her.
She saw again the farm, the muddy pond, her father in a smock under the apple trees, and she saw herself, as before, skimming the milk pans with her finger in the dairy.
But, with the flashes of the present moment, her past life, which had been so clear until then, was completely fading away, and she almost doubted having lived it.
She was there; then around the ball, there was nothing but shadow, spread over everything else.
She was then eating a maraschino ice, which she held in her left hand in a gilt shell, and she was half-closing her eyes, the spoon between her teeth.

sentences: Sir, this brave boy said to me, will you allow me to wish you a Happy New Year?
-- Of course, Conseil, just as if I were in Paris, in my office at the Jardin des Plantes.
I accept your wishes and I thank you for them.
However, I would like to ask you what you mean by 'a Happy New Year' given the circumstances we find ourselves in.
Is it the year that will bring an end to our imprisonment, or the year that will see this strange journey continue?
-- Indeed, replied Conseil, I don't really know what to say to you, sir.
It is certain that we are seeing curious things, and that for the past two months we haven't had time to be bored.
The latest wonder is always the most astonishing, and if this progression continues, I don't know how it will end.
I believe we will never find a similar opportunity again.
-- Never, Conseil.
-- Furthermore, sir Nemo, who truly justifies his Latin name, is no more bothersome than if he didn't exist.
-- As you say, Conseil.
I think, whether it pleases him or not, that a good year would be one that allows us to see everything...
See everything, Conseil?
That might take a while.
But what does Ned Land think?
Ned Land thinks exactly the opposite of me, replied Conseil.
He has a positive mindset and an insatiable appetite.
Looking at fish and always eating them is not enough for him.
The lack of wine, bread, and meat is hardly suitable for a worthy Saxon who is familiar with beefsteaks, and brandy or gin, taken in moderation, hardly frightens him!
As for me, Conseil, that's not what troubles me, and I get along very well with the ship's diet.
Me too, replied Conseil.
I think just as much about staying as Master Land does about fleeing.
So, if the coming year isn't good for me, it will be for him, and vice versa.
That way, there will always be someone satisfied.
Finally, to conclude, I wish you what will please you.
Thank you, Conseil.
However, I would ask you to postpone the question of the New Year's gifts and temporarily replace them with a good handshake.
I only have that on me.

sentences: Great misfortunes hardly sadden me, said Jean Bridelle, an old bachelor who was considered a skeptic.
I have seen the war up close: I stepped over bodies without compassion.

The strong brutalities of nature or of men can make us cry out in horror or indignation, but they do not give us that pang in the heart, that shiver that runs down your back at the sight of certain small, distressing things.
The most violent pain one can experience, certainly, is the loss of a child for a mother, and the loss of a mother for a man.
That is violent, terrible, it upsets and tears apart; but one heals from these catastrophes like from large, bleeding wounds.

Now, certain encounters, certain things glimpsed, guessed, certain secret sorrows, certain treacheries of fate, which stir up in us a whole painful world of thoughts, which suddenly open before us the mysterious door to moral sufferings, complicated, incurable, all the deeper because they seem benign, all the more acute because they seem almost elusive, all the more tenacious because they seem artificial, leave us with a trail of sadness in our soul, a taste of bitterness, a feeling of disenchantment that takes us a long time to shake off.
I always have before my eyes two or three things that others certainly would not have noticed, and which have entered me like long, thin, incurable stings.
You might not understand the emotion that has remained with me from these fleeting impressions.
I will only tell you one.
It is very old, but vivid as if it were yesterday.
It may be that only my imagination has contributed to my tenderness.
I am fifty years old.
I was young back then and I was studying law.
A little sad, a little dreamy, steeped in a melancholic philosophy, I didn't care much for noisy cafés, loud friends, or silly girls.
I would get up early; and one of my greatest pleasures was to take a solitary walk around eight in the morning in the Luxembourg nursery.
You haven't known it, have you, this nursery?
It was like a garden forgotten from the last century, a garden as lovely as a sweet smile of an old woman.
Thick hedges separated the narrow and regular paths, calm paths between two walls of meticulously trimmed foliage.

The gardener's large shears relentlessly aligned these partitions of branches; and, here and there, one would come across flowerbeds, borders of small trees lined up like schoolboys on a stroll, groups of magnificent rose bushes, or regiments of fruit trees.

sentences: A certain literary snobbery continues to rank readings, placing so-called demanding literature well above more accessible popular novels, which some consider almost shameful reading, barely tolerable on vacation.
This hierarchy deserves to be questioned rather than simply accepted as a cultural given.

It implicitly rests on the idea that a reading only has value if it requires significant intellectual effort, relegating the simple pleasure of reading to the status of a minor, almost guilty activity.
This conception, however, overlooks an important reality: reading, regardless of its formal complexity, fulfills multiple and legitimate functions that are not limited to intellectual exercise.
Pure narrative pleasure, temporary escape, and the relaxation provided by a predictable yet comforting plot are just as real benefits as the intellectual enrichment offered by a more demanding work.

Moreover, several studies in education sciences suggest that the pleasure of reading, regardless of the complexity level of the text in question, often serves as the necessary gateway to more regular reading practice and, eventually, to later, more demanding readings.
Prematurely imposing literature deemed 'serious' on someone who is just discovering the pleasure of reading could, paradoxically, discourage them from this practice in the long run.

Perhaps it would be wise to abandon this guilt-inducing hierarchy between noble and shameful readings, to simply recognize the legitimate diversity of functions that reading can fulfill, each meeting different but equally respectable needs, depending on the moments and the individuals involved.

sentences: However, according to the lieutenant's orders, the final preparations for winter were coming to an end.
They were busy ensuring there was enough food for the domestic animals for the duration of the long polar night.

The dogs were healthy and were getting fat doing nothing, but they couldn't be overly pampered, as the poor creatures would have to work terribly hard when they left Fort-Espérance to reach the continent across the ice field.
It was therefore important to keep them in perfect condition.
Thus, the fresh meat, especially the flesh of those reindeer that could be killed around the trading post, was not spared for them.
As for the domestic reindeer, they were thriving.
Their stable was suitably set up, and a considerable harvest of moss had been stored for them in the fort's supplies.
The females provided abundant milk to Mrs. Joliffe, who used it daily in her cooking preparations.
The corporal and his little wife had also replanted their crops, which had done so well during the warm season.
The ground had been prepared before the snow for the sorrel, scurvy grass, and Labrador tea plants.
These precious anti-scurvy foods were not to be lacking for the colony.
As for the wood, it filled the sheds up to the ridge.

The harsh and icy winter could now come, and the mercury column could freeze in the thermometer's bulb, without us being forced, as in the days of the last severe cold spells, to burn the furniture in the house.
