sentences: Behind our building, there had been an empty lot for years.
No one took care of it.
There was tall grass, some papers, and an old broken chair.
One day, the young man from the fourth floor had an idea.
During the neighbors' meeting, he proposed turning this lot into a shared garden.
At first, many people were against it.
"Who is going to take care of it?"
"It's going to cost money."
But he had prepared his project well.
He explained that the town hall provided assistance, and he suggested starting small: six vegetable plots.
After a long discussion, we voted yes, by a narrow margin.
We started in April.
At the beginning, there were seven of us: the young man, me, the elderly couple from the first floor, the family from the second floor, and Mrs. Renard, who complained but came every Saturday.
We cleaned the land, brought in soil, and built the wooden plots.
Each family takes care of one plot, but we all water them together.
This summer, we harvested tomatoes, zucchinis, salads, and a lot of herbs.
But the most interesting thing isn't the vegetables.
Before, I knew three neighbors.
Now, I know twelve.
And Mrs. Renard hardly complains anymore.

sentences: Ecology is all well and good, but it's a luxury for the rich.
This objection, often expressed with a hint of bitterness, reflects a reality that would be dishonest to ignore.
How can we ask someone who struggles to make ends meet to care about the planet?
The changes we advocate — consuming better, traveling differently, choosing more virtuous products — often come at a cost, and that cost primarily affects those who have the least.
The issue of social justice runs through the entire ecological question, and forgetting it would be a mistake.
There is some truth in this objection, and environmental advocates would be wrong to dismiss it.
Too many ecological discourses, delivered by comfortable people, ignore the constraints faced by those who have no choice.

Guilting someone for taking their car to work, when no public transport serves their village and they can't afford a clean vehicle, is not only unjust: it's politically absurd, because it turns against ecology those we would need.
But the idea that ecology would be a luxury is also based on a misleading reversal.
For it is precisely the most modest who suffer the most from environmental degradation.
They are the ones who live in the most polluted areas, who are hardest hit by heatwaves, floods, and the rising cost of energy and food.
Climate change is not a concern for aesthetes; it is a threat that primarily affects the most vulnerable.
In this sense, ecology is not the enemy of the poor, but their most direct interest.
The real problem is therefore not to choose between the end of the month and the end of the world, as a common saying puts it.
It is to reject this false dilemma.
An ecology that would worsen inequalities would be doomed to failure, as it would provoke rejection.
But a social justice that ignores the environment would condemn the most disadvantaged to be the first victims of disasters.
The two demands do not oppose each other; they must be held together.

Concretely, this means that the ecological transition must be just: that its costs do not weigh on the most vulnerable, that alternatives are made accessible to all, and that the effort required is proportionate to everyone's means.
An ecology that is not social condemns itself; a social policy that is not ecological prepares for worse injustices.
Ecology is only a luxury when it's misunderstood.
Well thought out, it is, on the contrary, what primarily protects those who have the least.

sentences: To philosophize is to learn how to die.
This phrase, which an essayist has taken from a long tradition, may seem morbid, as if wisdom consisted of being obsessed with death, living in its shadow.

Yet it expresses something profound, and almost the opposite of what one might initially believe: that meditating on death, far from darkening life, may actually be the condition for living it fully, and that wisdom, which is an art of living, is inseparably an art of dying.
Exploring this ancient phrase brings us closer to the heart of a wisdom that has endured through the centuries.
Let us first understand why meditation on death might be at the heart of wisdom.

Most of the time, we live in forgetfulness of death, as if we were never to die; this forgetfulness, as we have seen, fosters a certain unconsciousness of life, leading us to postpone what is essential and waste our days, which we believe to be countless.

Meditating on death, on the contrary, is to remember our finitude, and this memory changes everything: it makes us measure the value of time, distinguish the essential from the trivial, and live each moment as precious because it is limited.
Meditation on death does not darken life; it illuminates it, restoring the intensity that forgetfulness of death takes away.
This ancient tradition also teaches that meditation on death frees us from the fear of dying.
For this fear, which haunts us and poisons our lives, largely arises from our avoidance of the thought of death, which we repress and refuse to confront.
Those who meditate on it, tame it, and prepare for it can achieve a form of serenity and an acceptance that disarms fear.

Learning to die means learning to no longer fear death, to face it, to prepare for it rather than flee from it; and this preparation, far from being morbid, is liberating, as it frees us from the fear that otherwise dominates us.
We cannot free ourselves from death, but we can free ourselves from its fear; and it is through meditation that we achieve this.
There is more.
Meditation on death teaches us what truly matters by placing us in the perspective of the end.
Confronted with our death, realizing that our time is limited, we see more clearly what is worth dedicating our lives to and what is not.
Many things that worry us, agitate us, and obsess us then appear in their vanity; and what we neglected — loved ones, simple moments, what has meaning — reveals its true value.
Meditation on death is thus a school of discernment, separating the essential from the trivial, diverting us from vanities, and bringing us back to what matters.
Remembering that we will die is remembering to live for what is worthwhile.
This ancient wisdom is not a morbid cult of death, but rather an art of living fully.
For it contemplates death only to live better, considers the end only to give life its intensity, value, and meaning.

"Learning to die," from this perspective, is learning to live with full awareness of our finitude, not to waste our limited time, to cherish every moment as precious, to free ourselves from the poison of fear, and to discern what truly matters.
Meditation on death serves life; it is the detour through which we learn to truly live.
Far from being the enemy of the joy of living, it may actually be its condition, for it is the awareness of our finitude that gives life its value.
Thus, this ancient formula, which may initially seem morbid, reveals a profound and illuminating wisdom.
To philosophize is to learn to die, not to obsess over death, but to learn to live; not to darken life, but to illuminate it; not to fear the end, but to free ourselves from it.
Meditation on death is the heart of a wisdom that is an art of living, for it is by facing death that we learn the value of life.

And this lesson, perhaps the oldest, retains all its strength in our time, which flees from death, hides it, represses it, and in doing so, deprives itself of the awareness of finitude without which life loses its intensity and meaning.
Learning to die in order to learn to live: such is the wisdom with which we may need to begin and end.

sentences: From time to time, a guest as full as a barrel would step out to the nearby trees, relieve himself, and then return with a new hunger in his teeth.
The farmer's wives, flushed, oppressed, their bodices stretched tight like balloons, cut in two by their corsets, stayed at the table out of modesty.
But one of them, feeling more uncomfortable, went out, and then all of them got up in turn.
They returned happier, ready to laugh.
And the heavy jokes began.
They were bursts of obscenities thrown across the table, all about the wedding night.
The arsenal of the peasant's wit was emptied.
For a hundred years, the same risqué jokes had been used for the same occasions, and although everyone knew them, they still had an effect, sending the two rows of guests into loud laughter.
An old man with gray hair was calling out: 'Travelers for Mézidon by carriage.'
And there were screams of joy.
At the far end of the table, four guys, neighbors, were preparing pranks for the newlyweds, and they seemed to have a good one, so much so that they were stamping their feet while whispering.
One of them, suddenly taking advantage of a moment of calm, shouted:
It's the poachers who are going to have a field day tonight, with the moon that's out!...
Hey, Jean, isn't that the moon you're going to be watching?

sentences: He was no longer called anything in the whole region but 'that pig Morin,' and this epithet struck him like a sword each time he heard it.
When a thug in the street shouted, 'Pig,' he instinctively turned his head.
His friends bombarded him with horrible jokes, asking him every time they ate ham, 'Is it yours?'
He died two years later.
As for me, presenting myself for election in 1875, I went to pay a visit to the new notary of Tousserre, Me Belloncle.
A tall, wealthy, and beautiful woman received me.
'You don't recognize me?' she said.
I stammered, 'But... no... madam.'
--'Henriette Bonnel.'
--'Ah!'--And I felt myself go pale.
She seemed perfectly at ease and smiled as she looked at me.
As soon as she left me alone with her husband, he took my hands, squeezing them tightly: "It's been a long time, dear sir, that I've wanted to come see you.
My wife has talked so much about you.
I know... yes, I know under what painful circumstances you met her, and I also know how perfect you were, full of delicacy, tact, and devotion in the matter..."
He hesitated, then spoke more quietly, as if he were articulating a vulgar word, "... In the matter of that pig Morin."
